hero.title: Robotics that serves those who served.
hero.subtitle: We run hands-on robotics and engineering programs for veterans at the Milwaukee VA — building, programming, and fabricating alongside them. What started as a single introductory series has become an ongoing partnership: we are the only team ever invited back.

impact.label: Why it matters
impact.text: The Milwaukee VA has invited us back season after season — the only robotics team to earn a return invitation. Veterans and their families have even come out to volunteer and cheer at our Rookie Qualifier, turning a therapy program into a two-way community.

approach.label: Our Approach
approach.heading: Build-first. One-on-one. No experience needed.
approach.body:
Our veterans program is grounded in therapeutic recreation — the idea that purposeful, engaging activity is itself a form of healing. Rather than lecturing or demonstrating from a distance, every session is build-first: veterans have hardware in their hands within the first five minutes, and progress is measured in things they made rather than things they heard about. We match each participant with a GEarheads student mentor for one-on-one support throughout the session, so no one is left waiting for help or pushed past a comfortable pace.

That pairing is deliberate. Student mentors are close in age to junior veterans, and the dynamic is collaborative rather than instructional — two people figuring out a problem together, not a teacher and a student. We've found that veterans who come in skeptical of robotics relax quickly once they realize the goal is to build something that works, not to pass a test. The FLL and SPIKE platforms we use are forgiving: failed builds tell you exactly what to fix, which makes iteration feel natural rather than discouraging.

Over two six-week series, the program is designed to build on itself. Each week's session references what participants made the week before, so skills accumulate rather than reset. By the time veterans reach the CAD/CNC sign-building program in the second series, they are applying design thinking that started with LEGO motors and mission fields — a progression that mirrors how our own team trains new members.

programs.label: Intro FLL Challenge
programs.summary: An accessible first step into robotics.
programs.detail: The program opens with FIRST LEGO League — the same entry-level robotics platform that launches elementary and middle-school students into FIRST. Veterans work in small groups to build a LEGO robot from the ground up and program it to complete a series of missions on a themed competition field. We chose FLL deliberately as the on-ramp: it needs no prior engineering background, every session ends with something that visibly works, and progress is easy to feel week over week. Our student mentors sit alongside each participant, breaking builds and code into small, achievable steps so the focus stays on problem-solving and confidence rather than on the technology itself. The competitive structure of FLL missions also gives each session a clear win condition — which turns what could feel like an abstract exercise into something with genuine stakes and satisfaction.
highlights: Build a working LEGO robot from the ground up
Program it to complete missions on a themed FLL field
No prior robotics or coding experience required
One-on-one support from student mentors every session

programs.label: CAD/CNC Sign-Building
programs.summary: Design it on a screen, cut it on a real machine.
programs.detail: The second program bridges the digital and the physical. Veterans learn the fundamentals of computer-aided design, sketching and refining a custom sign on-screen, then watch that same design come to life on one of our CNC machines. Taking a project from an idea, to a CAD model, to toolpaths, to a finished piece of material demystifies the manufacturing process the team uses on its own competition robots. It is deliberately tangible: participants leave holding something they designed and machined themselves — a personalized sign they get to keep — which makes the leap from software to real fabrication click in a way a lecture never could. The CAD/CNC sessions are also the moment many veterans first realize that the tools used to build competition robots are within reach of anyone who can use a computer, not just trained engineers.
highlights: Design a personalized sign from a blank canvas
See the design machined on a real CNC mill
Leave with a finished, physical project to keep

programs.label: Advanced FLL Spike
programs.summary: A step up in building and code.
programs.detail: For returning veterans ready for more, the advanced series moves up to LEGO SPIKE Prime — a richer platform with more capable motors, a wider sensor set, and a deeper programming environment. Sessions push past following instructions into genuine engineering thinking: reading sensor feedback, writing conditional logic, and designing mechanisms that solve a specific problem. Because it builds directly on the foundation from the intro series, participants get to see how far the fundamentals they already learned can scale, and they take on challenges that would have felt out of reach on day one. The SPIKE Prime platform is also the same category of hardware that FTC teams around the state are building with — so veterans who complete the advanced series have genuine, transferable skills in robotics programming.
highlights: Advanced building and programming with LEGO SPIKE Prime
Design mechanisms that solve a defined problem
Builds directly on the intro FLL foundation
A clear progression for returning participants

howItRuns.label: Six-Week Series
howItRuns.desc: The program runs as two dedicated six-week series across the season — one introductory and one advanced. Each series has a clear arc: skills from week one carry forward and build on themselves, so participants arrive knowing what to expect and leave with a sense of sustained progress rather than isolated one-off activities.

howItRuns.label: Weekly Sessions
howItRuns.desc: Twelve weekly sessions in total, each running approximately 90 minutes. The consistent schedule — same day, same time, same mentors — matters as much as the content. Predictability reduces the friction of showing up, and the rhythm of a weekly practice is what turns individual lessons into a skill set.

howItRuns.label: Hands-On
howItRuns.desc: Every session is build-first: hardware is on the table and in participants' hands within the first few minutes. There are no slide decks or passive lectures. Student mentors work alongside veterans one-on-one — breaking down a build step, debugging a line of code, or thinking through why a mechanism isn't behaving as expected — so the work stays active throughout the full 90 minutes.
